concepts.name: Scaling Laws
concepts.definition: Empirical relationships showing how model performance (e.g., cross-entropy loss) changes predictably as scale factors like model size, dataset size, or compute increase, following a power-law function.
concepts.intuition: Like turning up the volume on a speaker—each time you double the size, performance improves by a predictable amount, not randomly.
concepts.importance: They enable prediction and optimization of AI performance without exhaustive experimentation, guiding efficient resource allocation.
concepts.example: Doubling model parameters reduces loss by 20% consistently across scales from 1M to 1B parameters.

concepts.name: Power Law
concepts.definition: A mathematical relationship where one quantity varies as a power of another, expressed as Y = k * X^a, where k and a are constants.
concepts.intuition: Think of it like compound interest—each increase in scale multiplies performance gains by a fixed factor, not adds a fixed amount.
concepts.importance: Enables extrapolation of model performance far beyond observed data, forming the foundation for predictive scaling in AI.
concepts.example: Loss decreases as N^(-0.07) where N is model size—small changes in scale lead to predictable loss improvements.

concepts.name: Model Size (N)
concepts.definition: The number of non-embedding parameters in a neural language model, determining its capacity to learn patterns.
concepts.intuition: Like the number of brain cells—a bigger model can store more knowledge and make finer distinctions.
concepts.importance: Larger models are significantly more sample-efficient and drive the majority of performance gains under fixed compute.
concepts.example: A 1B-parameter model outperforms a 10M-parameter model on the same dataset with far fewer training steps.

concepts.name: Dataset Size (D)
concepts.definition: The total number of tokens or data points used to train the language model.
concepts.intuition: More books read = smarter student. More data gives the model more examples to learn from.
concepts.importance: Limits how much a model can generalize; insufficient data causes overfitting even with large models.
concepts.example: Training a 10B-parameter model on only 1GB of text leads to poor generalization compared to training it on 100GB.

concepts.name: Compute Budget (C)
concepts.definition: The total amount of computational resources (measured in FLOPs or PF-days) allocated for training a model.
concepts.intuition: Think of it as the total time and electricity you’re willing to spend—more compute lets you train longer, bigger, or both.
concepts.importance: Determines the trade-off between model size, data volume, and training duration for optimal performance.
concepts.example: With 100 PF-days, you can train a small model to convergence or a huge model for a few steps—latter often performs better.

concepts.name: Sample Efficiency
concepts.definition: The ability of a model to achieve high performance using fewer training samples or optimization steps.
concepts.intuition: A smart student learns from one example where others need ten—large models extract more knowledge per data point.
concepts.importance: Enables cost-effective training by reducing data and compute needs, critical for scaling to real-world datasets.
concepts.example: A 1B-parameter model reaches the same loss as a 10M-parameter model using only 1/10th of the training data.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: When a model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data due to memorizing noise instead of learning patterns.
concepts.intuition: Like a student who memorizes answers for a test but can’t answer new questions—too big for the data.
concepts.importance: Scaling laws show overfitting is predictable: it happens when model size grows faster than data size.
concepts.example: A 10B-parameter model trained on 1GB of text overfits; increasing data to 5GB fixes it without changing model size.

concepts.name: Compute-Efficient Training
concepts.definition: Training strategy that maximizes performance per unit of computational cost by prioritizing model size over training time or data.
concepts.intuition: Instead of running a small car for 10 hours, drive a racecar for 2 hours—bigger models extract more value from limited compute.
concepts.importance: Reveals that large models trained briefly outperform small ones trained to convergence under fixed compute.
concepts.example: Using 10 PF-days to train a 10B-parameter model for 1% of its convergence time yields better results than training a 1M-model to full convergence.

concepts.name: Optimal Allocation
concepts.definition: The strategy of distributing a fixed compute budget across model size, dataset size, and training time to maximize performance.
concepts.intuition: Like budgeting for a road trip—you can spend on gas, food, or time; the best trip balances all three optimally.
concepts.importance: Guides practical AI development by showing where to invest compute for maximum return.
concepts.example: With 100 PF-days, allocate 70% to model size, 25% to data, and 5% to extended training steps for best results.

concepts.name: Training Curve
concepts.definition: A plot showing how model loss decreases over training time (steps or compute), revealing learning dynamics.
concepts.intuition: Like a student’s grades over the semester—initial steep improvement, then gradual plateau.
concepts.importance: Power laws in training curves allow early prediction of final performance, saving time and resources.
concepts.example: After 10% of training steps, loss trend predicts final loss within 5%, even if training continues for 10x longer.

concepts.name: Convergence
concepts.definition: The point in training where model loss stops decreasing significantly, indicating full learning under current conditions.
concepts.intuition: Like a ball rolling downhill—it eventually stops at the bottom. But sometimes, stopping early is better.
concepts.importance: Contrary to intuition, optimal training often stops well before convergence when scaling models.
concepts.example: A 10B-parameter model reaches peak performance at 5% of convergence steps—training further wastes compute.

concepts.name: Model Shape
concepts.definition: Architectural details like depth (layers) vs. width (neurons per layer), which have minimal impact on performance compared to scale.
concepts.intuition: It’s not about the shape of your toolbox, but how many tools you have—scale matters more than structure.
concepts.importance: Allows simplification of hyperparameter tuning; focus on size, not architecture tweaks.
concepts.example: Two models with 100M parameters—one deep, one wide—perform nearly identically on language tasks.

concepts.name: Transfer Performance
concepts.definition: Model performance on data from a different distribution than the training set, indicating generalization ability.
concepts.intuition: A student who does well on math tests also does well on physics—same skill, different context.
concepts.importance: Shows that gains in training performance transfer predictably to new domains with a constant penalty.
concepts.example: A model trained on Wikipedia but tested on medical journals still improves proportionally to its training loss, with a fixed 0.2 loss penalty.

concepts.name: Gradient Noise Scale
concepts.definition: A measure of the variability in gradients during training, used to determine optimal batch size.
concepts.intuition: Like measuring how noisy a radio signal is—higher noise means you need to listen longer (larger batch) to get clear signals.
concepts.importance: Enables automatic tuning of batch size for optimal training efficiency without manual experimentation.
concepts.example: For a 10B-parameter model, optimal batch size is ~1.5M tokens because gradient noise stabilizes at that scale.

concepts.name: Infinite Data Limit
concepts.definition: The theoretical performance ceiling of a model when trained on an infinitely large dataset, isolating the effect of model size.
concepts.intuition: If you had every book ever written, how good could your model get? This is the theoretical best with perfect data.
concepts.importance: Helps separate limits of model capacity from limits of data availability, guiding future scaling goals.
concepts.example: Even with infinite data, a 1B-parameter model has higher loss than a 10B one—model size still caps performance.
